title: Chicken enchiladas
skill: Scaling a recipe from 4 to 12 by hand

notes.text: One 9-by-13-inch dish holds 12 enchiladas, enough for 4. For 12 people, use three dishes and rotate them halfway through baking.

move.title: Written for 4, cooked for 12
move.body: Red chile enchiladas start with a sauce of toasted dried guajillo chiles, blended smooth. This recipe is written for 4. This week you'll scale it to 12 by hand on paper, check your numbers against the app, and decide what doesn't simply triple: salt, spice, time, and pans.

why.title: The scaling factor
why.body: New servings divided by old servings: 12 ÷ 4 = 3. Every ingredient is multiplied by it. Counted items round sensibly: 3 × 3 garlic cloves is 9.

why.title: What doesn't triple
why.body: Salt and chile heat build up faster than you expect in a big batch, so start at about two and a half times and taste. Simmering time grows only a little; baking time stays the same per dish. Pans don't stretch: three batches need three dishes or a much bigger pot.

why.title: Toast the chiles briefly
why.body: A few seconds a side in a dry pan wakes up a dried chile's oils. A few seconds too long and it scorches and turns the whole sauce bitter.

why.title: Soften the tortillas
why.body: Cold corn tortillas crack when rolled. A few seconds in a lightly oiled pan makes them pliable, and the oil keeps them from turning soggy in the sauce.

wrong.fix: The chiles scorched. Start the sauce again; bitterness doesn't cook out.
Warm them longer in the pan, and roll them while warm.

wrong.sign: The big batch is too salty
wrong.fix: Add more unsalted broth and simmer a few minutes. Next time, salt at two and a half times, then taste.
Rotate the dishes halfway through baking, and check the middle with the thermometer.

quiz.q: What's the scaling factor from 4 to 12?
Which of these shouldn't be simply tripled?
Does a tripled recipe bake three times as long?
choices: No, about the same per dish
quiz.explain: Each dish is the same size.

quiz.q: Why toast the chiles only a few seconds?
choices: They scorch and turn bitter fast

steps.text: Scale the recipe to 12 on paper: multiply every amount by 3. Then set the servings to 12 and compare your list with the app's.
steps.tip: Write salt at two and a half times, and plan three baking dishes.

steps.text: Put the chicken in the saucepan, cover it by 1 inch with water, and add the chicken's salt.
Wash your hands with hot, soapy water.
Bring it to a boil, then simmer, partly covered.
Meanwhile, cut the stems off the chiles, slit them, and shake out the seeds.
Toast the chiles in the dry skillet over medium heat, pressing flat with the tongs, 10 to 15 seconds a side.
steps.look: Fragrant and slightly darker, not smoking.

steps.text: Heat the broth until steaming, pour it over the chiles in the heatproof bowl, and let them soak.
Lift out the thickest thigh and check it. It needs to read at least 165°F. If not, simmer 3 minutes more.
Cool the chicken on the plate for 5 minutes, then shred it with two forks.
Dice the onion and mince the garlic. Soften them in the sauce's oil in the large pot over medium heat.
Add the chiles and their broth, the tomato paste, cumin, oregano, and the sauce's salt. Blend smooth with the stick blender, blade kept under.
Simmer the sauce, stirring now and then, until it coats a spoon. Taste for salt.
Warm the enchiladas' oil in the skillet over medium heat. Pass each tortilla through it, 5 seconds a side, and stack them on the plate.
Spread a cup of sauce in the baking dish. Roll each tortilla around chicken and a little cheese, and lay it seam side down.
Pour the rest of the sauce over the top, scatter on the remaining cheese, and cover with foil.
Bake covered, then uncover and bake until the cheese browns in spots.
steps.look: Sauce bubbling at the edges, cheese melted and spotted brown.

steps.text: Rest 5 minutes, then serve with cilantro and sour cream.
